https://www.bridgwatermercury.co.uk/news.text: Column: Brian Smedley on opposing the far-right in Somerset By Cllr Brian Smedley Share 0 Comments "Britain has had a 10-year spiral of large numbers of people moving further to the right, largely because they haven’t sussed where the direction of travel will lead them" (Image: Cllr Brian Smedley) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. The Daleks are a fictitious race of intergalactic robots, writes Cllr Brian Smedley . In Bridgewater Place in Leeds, there’s a giant building overlooking Holbeck Moor called ‘The Dalek’. The Daleks are a highly xenophobic neo-fascist regime who seek to destroy all non-Dalek life in the universe. I don’t think I’m struggling for metaphors here…fascists sadly aren’t fictitious. In 1936, Leeds anti-fascists assembled here to kick Oswald Mosley and his British Union of Fascists out of Leeds. A week later, the more well-known Battle of Cable Street happened when Moseley tried to march through the predominantly Jewish communities of that part of East London. They were met by anti-fascists who outnumbered them, and the tradition of standing up against fascism became embedded in our culture. Socialists, radicals, liberals, trade unionists, migrant communities, the working class all knew and know that unity is strength, and fascism is division and destruction. In many cases, ‘extermination’. Fascists have always done this. They’re not respectable in their own right - everyone who saw the death camps, the gas chambers, the repression, the wars, the executions, all know what fascism means. So, they try to latch onto other ideas and groups as a cover. In 1986, fascists tried to hijack a ‘Friends of British Ulster’ march through Bridgwater . This was a protest against Tom King, Bridgwater MP of the day and then Northern Ireland secretary, who was trying, modestly, to equalise the power balance in Northern Ireland at the time and annoying both communities. Whether you support Ulster being British or Ulster being Irish, either view is legitimate. But because the fascists of the day tried to hijack the march, we organised a counter-protest. The police provided a security cordon of four. When the first ‘fascist’ was arrested (he later stood for the National Front in a parliamentary by-election), the police realised they’d under-calculated and couldn’t arrest anyone else. The march turned into a bit of a scrap. Read more Brian Smedley: Mythbusting what really happens in local government Brian Smedley: Bridgwater and the Czech Republic's music scene is intertwined Brian Smedley column: Farage vs a bin - I know who'd have my vote Last weekend, I joined a protest in Taunton organised by Somerset anti-racists which included trades unionists and community groups. The ‘far-right’ group was targeting ‘illegal migrants’ and ‘two-tier policing’. But they said they weren’t far right. It didn’t help when the leader of Britain First, an actual far-right group, Paul Golding, was advertised to speak. He didn’t turn up. And it got worse when one of their local members was filmed clearly saying the problem was the increase in the number of black children in the schools. To define far right, you go back to its origins. During the French Revolution, the groups that wanted change, equality, liberalisation and power to the lower classes sat on the left, and the groups that were happy with the status quo and supported the traditional system, the landed gentry and the aristocracy, sat on the right. The divisions have persisted, so today if you put the Lib Dems in the centre, Labour and the Greens are to the left, and the Tories are to the right. Communists and anarchists, you can call far left and anything from Reform through Restore to the actual neo-fascist groups on the murky fringe of politics are clearly far right. They’ll never come to power unless they convince the majority that they are credible… and ‘not fascist’. How do we challenge and expose them? Holbeck Moor, Cable Street, well, unity and solidarity plus facts and information are always a useful starting point. However…when I turned up at the demo the first thing I saw was Lib Dem Cllr Richard Wilkins with a bunch of flowers. "Ha ha!" I said, "You should try giving them to the fascists!" "Yes," he said, "That’s what I’m going to do." He wasn’t joking. I had this vision of the Blackshirts marching towards the barricades in Cable Street armed with clubs and batons to be met by a line of workers suddenly putting down their fists and producing daffodils and tulips and everyone suddenly loving each other. In November 1989, Czech students calling for the downfall of communism marched up Narodni Street in Prague, and when they met the line of riot police, they sat down, lit candles and gave them flowers. The police battered them. Wilkins gave the leader of the march a hug. They did engage. It was filmed. I wondered: 'If only someone had thought of this at the siege of Stalingrad…’ Meanwhile, this time the police had over 100 on the streets, and they kept the two sides apart. I counted 69 in the far right/‘we’re not far-right’ group and 250 in the ‘you are far right/no far right in Taunton!’ group. Britain has had a 10-year spiral of large numbers of people moving further to the right. Largely because they haven’t sussed where the direction of travel will lead them. But the evidence is in the groupings that these parties made when lined up alongside their European sister parties. UKIP and the Brexit Party all lined up in the EU with the far-right groups that were and are on the rise in other European states. Both were rebranded in whatever current image Nigel Farage has. I’d say it’s far right. They’re certainly not as soft and cuddly as…er…the Conservative Party. That said, they did have quite a lot of Tories join them in the last year…the jury’s out. Photograph: Mohammed Salha/APAImages/Shutterstock Gaza Pregnant woman among more than 10 killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza Woman’s family says she died of injuries after being shot in the head while sitting inside a tent near Khan Younis Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem and Seham Tantesh in Gaza Sun 13 Sep 2026 11.51 EDT Last modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 15.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A pregnant Palestinian woman died on Saturday from injuries sustained after being shot in the head by Israeli forces south of Khan Younis, according to her family and medical workers, as strikes across Gaza killed at least 10 people in 48 hours. The woman, named as Iman Shalouf, 27, who was nearly eight months pregnant, was sitting inside her family’s tent in the al-Mawasi area when Israeli gunfire struck her, according to paramedics and witnesses. ‘‘We heard the sound of gunfire while I was praying,’’ Wathfa abu Mashi, Shalouf’s mother-in-law, said in a video interview with Anadolu . “My daughter asked me, ‘Where is Iman?’ I told her she was in her tent. She went to check on her and found her covered in blood after she was hit by a bullet.” Shalouf’s husband, Ismail abu Mashi, said “Where is the ceasefire they keep talking about? There is no such thing. There is killing every day. People are dying here every day.” Shalouf was rushed to Nasser hospital, where doctors initially detected her unborn baby’s heartbeat, but she and her unborn baby died a few hours later. According to relatives, Shalouf had already chosen the name Ayoub for the baby, who was due in November. Relatives and community members gathered at the hospital to hold funeral prayers for Shalouf and her child before carrying their bodies for burial in Khan Younis. They were buried side by side. Contacted by the Guardian, the Israel Defense Forces said they were looking into the incident. Despite the ceasefire agreement reached in October 2025, violence and the killing of Palestinians continue on a daily basis. The health ministry in Gaza said 10 Palestinians had been killed and 56 wounded in Israeli attacks over the previous 48 hours , amid artillery shelling and gunfire in several areas of northern, central and southern Gaza. View image in fullscreen Displaced Palestinians walk among the ruins of buildings in al-Sheikh Radwan neighbourhood east of Gaza City. Photograph: Mohammed Saber/EPA Four members of the same family – Momen Ahmed, his wife, Haneen Saleh, and their daughters Lana, 12, and Bana, eight – were killed when their home in Beit Lahiya was struck on Thursday night, according to the ministry. Six other Palestinians were reported killed in Khan Younis and Gaza City on Friday, including a man who died of wounds sustained in an earlier attack. Several other Palestinians were injured in attacks across Gaza. On Friday, two people were reportedly seriously injured in an attack in Beit Lahiya, while three people including a woman six months pregnant and a child were wounded by gunfire in the same city. On Saturday, nine people were injured when a displaced people’s tent in al-Mawasi was shelled, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent. On Sunday, two Palestinians were killed and several others injured when a vehicle was struck in Tel al-Hawa in Gaza City, according to the health ministry. The attack also injured people on a passing bus carrying women and children. On 28 August, Unicef said at least four children had been reported killed in the preceding five days and many others wounded, including children who sustained life-changing injuries. On 2 September, it said three other children had reportedly been killed and at least five others injured in the preceding 24 hours, bringing the number of children reportedly killed between 23 August and 2 September to seven. “Airstrikes by Israeli forces continue killing and wounding Palestinians,” Médecins Sans Frontières said . “Between September 6 and 9, Israeli forces issued 18 so-called evacuation orders and struck a building less than 250ft from an MSF clinic.” The humanitarian situation remains severe. According to the UN’s humanitarian office, “most of Gaza’s 2.1 million are approaching the rainy season in overcrowded displacement sites, at risk of flooding and disease, while efforts to help them prepare are constrained by funding shortfalls and access restrictions”. On 31 August, a temporary halt to desalination in Israel reduced the water available to about a million people in Gaza who rely on the Israeli grid. Several electricity generators at hospitals across the Gaza Strip have stopped working because of shortages of spare parts and fuel, the territory’s health ministry has said. According to the ministry, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the fragile ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025. Since Israel’s war in Gaza began on 7 October 2023, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to the ministry. https://miningdigital.com/news/siemens-s.text: Article Automation & AI Siemens Showcases Digital Process In Canada By Nick Edstrom September 22, 2026 undefined mins Share this article Prioritise Us on Google Share this article Prioritise Us on Google Rendering of the Red Rock lithium converter plant design. Canadian developer Rock Tech Lithium is collaborating with Siemens Canada to develop a digital process twin of its Red Rock converter project in Ontario Siemens Canada has inked a contract with Rock Tech to provide a digital process twin to support an ongoing definitive feasibility study for its Red Rock lithium converter project in Ontario. “The partnership with Siemens strengthens German-Canadian cooperation and supports Rock Tech's objective of establishing the Red Rock Converter as a strategic contributor to resilient G7 critical minerals supply chains,” says Rock Tech CEO Mirco Wojnarowicz. Siemens Canada will initially implement a digital process twin, but the two parties plan to extend the Digital Twin technology to cover the entire project lifecycle: from the feasibility study through engineering and construction to operations. Mirco Wojnarowicz, Chief Executive Officer of Rock Tech Siemens' Digital Twin technology creates a virtual, physics-based model of the plant's processes, energy flows, and material streams, enabling Rock Tech to test, optimise, and validate design choices, efficiency, emissions, and operational reliability before major capital is committed. The award sits within a broader memorandum of understanding signed between the developer and Siemens Canada in March, which is designed to bring German lithium conversion expertise and industrial digitalisation technology to the Red Rock converter project. Siemens Canada will also support Rock Tech's project team by providing specialised support in Process Control, Instrumentation and Automation Architecture as part of the ongoing DFS for the Red Rock Converter. The DFS was launched at the end of June 2026 and is expected to be finalised by mid-December 2026. Rock Tech’s lithium projects Lithium is a foundational material for electrification, renewable power generation and electric vehicles, making it a priority commodity for companies positioning themselves for the energy transition. Rock Tech is developing domestic supply chains of locally produced lithium in Germany and in Canada to supply battery and automotive industries with battery grade material sourced from sustainable value chains. The company is developing two lithium converter projects: the first in Guben, Germany is intended to produce up to 24,000 tonnes of lithium hydroxide monohydrate per year and the second in Red Rock, Ontario, is intended to produce up to 32,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent per year. Rock Tech Lithium plans to source raw material from its own Georgia Lake spodumene mining project in the Thunder Bay Mining District of Ontario. Rock Tech's Guben lithium converter project in Brandenburg, Germany. Rock Tech's key business partners: ArcelorMittal ArcelorMittal is one of the world's leading integrated steel and mining companies with a presence in 60 countries and primary steelmaking operations in 15 countries. It is the largest steel producer in Europe, among the largest in the Americas, and has a growing presence in Asia through a joint venture in India. ArcelorMittal Eisenhüttenstadt, a subsidiary located in Brandenburg in Germany, signed a letter of intent with Rock Tech in October 2025. BMI BMI Group is a real estate development and revitalisation company specializing in the adaptive reuse and repurposing of end-of-use industrial and commercial properties and their transition from linear to circular economies. The former Red Rock mill site is being developed in partnership with the Red Rock Indian Band (RRIB), an Ojibwe First Nation in Northwestern Ontario, as a catalyst for the town of Red Rock and the greater Nipigon region. Transamine Transamine is an independent and privately held commodity trading company specializing in non-ferrous raw materials. Transamine is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland. Transamine is a full-service company providing worldwide raw material sourcing, marketing, finance, and investment and specialises in all aspects of non-ferrous raw materials, as well as lithium in the form of spodumene, production and trade. https://www.digi24.ro/stiri/externe/rusi.text: Direcția Generală de Informații a Ministerului Apărării din Ucraina a publicat pe portalul War&Sanctions rezultatele unei analize a structurii dronei „Geran-5 K5-K”, precum și o listă cu aproape o sută de componente electronice de producție străină. Potrivit serviciului de presă al GUR , la începutul toamnei acestui an, trupele ruse au început să utilizeze o nouă versiune a „Geran-5” pentru a lansa atacuri asupra orașelor ucrainene. Din punct de vedere al schemei aerodinamice și al caracteristicilor tactico-tehnice, acest aparat poate fi deja clasificat în categoria rachetelor cu aripi de dimensiuni reduse. Specialiștii GUR au examinat una dintre aceste drone, care, din motive necunoscute, a căzut aproape intactă în mijlocul unui câmp ucrainean. Planorul „Geran-5 K5-K”, la fel ca versiunea anterioară, are o configurație aerodinamică clasică. Aripile sale drepte, în formă de săgeată, sunt amplasate în partea superioară a fuselajului, iar trenul de coadă este format dintr-o singură chila, stabilizatoare fixe și o cârma de direcție. Noua variantă a devenit mai compactă decât predecesoarea sa: lungimea fuselajului a scăzut de la 6,5 la 4 metri, iar anvergura aripilor – de la 3,2 la 3 metri. În același timp, inginerii ruși au îmbunătățit caracteristicile aerodinamice ale fuselajului pentru a crește viteza și altitudinea de zbor. Altitudinea maximă de zbor a modelului K5-K a crescut de la 5 la 6 km. Viteza de croazieră depășește 450 km/h, iar în timpul anumitor manevre aparatul poate atinge viteze de până la 1000 km/h. În același timp, autonomia de zbor a rămas la 1000 km, iar masa încărcăturii de luptă – la 90 kg. În eșantionul analizat, cercetătorii au descoperit, printre altele, o încărcătură termobarică de tip TBBCH-90. Sistemul avionic K5-K este similar cu cel utilizat în ultimele versiuni ale unei alte drone cu reacție – „Geran-4 Seeker”. Aceasta include un controler de zbor, un sistem de navigație inerțial SADRA Seeker cu modulul MOX, o copie localizată a antenei CRP Harxon GI-006 cu 16 elemente, un tracker, un modem mesh și alte componente. În plus, în aparat a fost descoperit un nou bloc al sistemului de corelație opto-electronic „Susanin” – anterior, GUR identificase deja acest sistem în dronele „Geran-4”. Aceasta compară imaginile obținute de la senzorul optic cu imaginea de referință stocată în memoria microcomputerului. Acest lucru permite verificarea conformității traseului rachetei sau a dronei cu traiectoria prestabilită, de la locul de lansare până la țintă. În modelul K5-K analizat, în locul senzorilor optici, sistemul „Susanin” a utilizat o cameră cu dublă bandă. Microcomputerul Coke Pi – un echivalent chinezesc al Raspberry Pi – procesează direct imaginile și le compară cu imaginea de referință. Acesta este amplasat într-o carcasă din plastic cu marcajul corespunzător. Urmărește știrile Digi24.ro și pe Google News
